{"self_assessment": "Impact: I chose the fish and drew the full sketch on the pad at the start: body top, belly and tail as three strokes, with the nose as the start and the tail branching off where the body lines meet. Choosing a simple, readable outline with big shapes and gentle curves is what let the table build quickly and kept the picture recognizable. About 108 of 111 dominoes were connected to the start at the push, and the only unconnected ones were a few strays near the nose that don't affect the outline.

Execution: I designed the sketch around what dominoes can do: rounded curves, gentle branching, and a single start where all lines leave in the same direction. I inspected the middle crossing and the surrounding body repeatedly to check that the fall carried through the whole fish, and I stood a domino back up in the middle section. Before the push I did a final check of the crossing and confirmed it held.

Collaboration: I split the work into strokes on the first call, so all three teammates started building within the first minute with no overlap. I kept the group clear on who had which area, asked people to keep hands off finished sections to avoid bumps, and left the nose joint to the teammate already working on it so we didn't get in each other's way.

Leadership: I set the plan in the first seconds: the animal, the sketch, and who traced which stroke. I kept the table coordinated through the build with short status updates and a clear hands-off rule near the end. The result was a finished, connected fish well before the push.", "my_share_percent": 35}
